I THE UNEXPECTED GUEST

Pip the squirrel was quite certain he was the cleverest creature in the whole yard. He had buried more acorns than he could count, and he could climb the tall oak tree to his nest in the blink of an eye. He was taking a moment to rest on a low branch, twitching his nose proudly, when Old Man Thistle, the woodchuck who lived under the garden shed, shuffled by.

"You look mighty pleased with yourself, Pip," the woodchuck rumbled, his voice low and earthy. "Did you find a whole bag of walnuts that the blue jays missed?"

"Better than that!" Pip chittered. "I have arranged my winter stores so perfectly that I shall not want for a single meal. I have a system, you see. It is all about planning."

"Is that so?" Old Man Thistle said with a slow blink. "Well, planning is a fine thing. But sometimes the unexpected happens. What is your plan for that?"

Pip flicked his tail. "There is nothing I cannot handle!" he declared. But just as the words left his mouth, he saw something that made him freeze. A new creature was in the yard. It was small and gray, with a long, thin tail and a pointed face. And it was heading directly for the big oak tree!

"Who is that?" Pip whispered, his fur standing on end. "He is an intruder!"

Old Man Thistle squinted. "Why, that's a possum. A young one, by the looks of him. He probably just wandered over from the woods."

"Well, he cannot stay here!" Pip insisted. "This is my tree!" He scurried down the trunk to confront the stranger, who had stopped and was looking up with wide, worried eyes. "You there!" Pip squeaked, trying to sound as fierce as possible. "You must leave at once! This territory is taken!"

The little possum simply trembled. "I'm lost," he said in a tiny voice. "My mother told me to wait for her if I got separated, and this tree looked very tall and safe."

Pip was about to tell him to find a different tree when Old Man Thistle ambled up beside him. "Now, now, Pip," he said gently. "The little fellow is only lost. He is not trying to steal your acorns. There is room enough in the yard for one more, just for a little while."

Pip looked at the frightened possum, and then at the kindly woodchuck. "Oh, very well!" he grumbled. "But only until his mother comes! And he is not to touch my nuts!"

II A LESSON IN SHARING

The little possum, whose name was Percy, curled up in a small hollow at the base of the oak tree and waited. Pip watched him from a branch above, his tail twitching with suspicion. He saw Percy shiver as a cool breeze rustled the leaves.

"Hmph!" Pip muttered to himself. "It is a bit chilly down there." He remembered the soft, warm lining of his own nest, full of scavenged bits of cloth and fluff. He tried to go back to thinking about his perfect winter stores, but the sight of the shivering little creature bothered him.

Old Man Thistle was busy digging near the edge of the vegetable patch. "A fine evening for digging," he called up to Pip. "The soil is nice and soft."

"Percy is cold," Pip said, surprising himself.

"Is he now?" the woodchuck said, pausing his work. "Well, that is a shame. A cold night for a little one far from his own bed." He went back to his digging.

Pip fidgeted. He scampered to a different branch. He groomed his whiskers. Finally, he could stand it no longer. He scurried down the tree. "You!" he said to Percy, who looked up with startled eyes. "Are you hungry?"

"A little," Percy whispered.

With a great sigh, as if he were making a huge sacrifice, Pip ran to one of his secret caches. He dug up a single, perfect acorn and rolled it over to the little possum. "Here," he said gruffly. "But do not expect any more."

Percy nibbled the acorn gratefully. "Thank you," he said. "You are very kind."

"I am not kind!" Pip snapped, though he felt a strange warmth spreading through his chest. "I am simply practical! A hungry guest makes too much noise!"

Just then, a soft rustling came from the hedgerow. A much larger possum poked her head out. "Percy?" she called softly. "There you are, my dear! I was so worried!"

Percy jumped up and ran to his mother's side. He turned and gave a happy little wave to Pip. "The squirrel gave me a nut, Mama!" he cried.

His mother smiled warmly at Pip. "Thank you for looking after my boy," she said, before she and Percy disappeared back into the shadows of the woods.

Pip watched them go. The yard felt very quiet now. He looked at the empty spot where Percy had been, and then at his own paws. "Well," he said to Old Man Thistle, who had watched the whole thing. "I suppose the unexpected is not always so bad."

"No, indeed," the old woodchuck rumbled. "Sometimes, it brings an opportunity. And sometimes," he added with a chuckle, "it even brings a new friend, if only for an evening."

The white mare tossed her head, her nostrils flaring. "Humph! Mind my own business indeed! When a frightened colt is about to bolt and cause trouble for everyone, it becomes my business. A smithy is no place for skittish little things."

Before Twinkleheels could think of another sharp reply, old Ebenezer spoke. His voice was as calm and deep as the water in the farm pond on a summer evening. "Now, now," he said gently, looking at the white mare. "There is a first time for every horse in a smithy. I seem to recall a story about a certain young mare who was so nervous on her first visit that she kicked over the water tub."

The white mare's ears went back. "I never! That's a dreadful story and it isn't true!" she declared, though she shuffled her feet a bit.

"Hold still, you!" the blacksmith commanded from her side. He was holding one of her hind feet between his knees. "Do you want to leave here with only three shoes? A few more wiggles and you will."

The mare fell silent at once, pressing her lips together in a firm line. She gave Ebenezer one last cross look, but she did not say another word.

Twinkleheels watched, feeling a little thrill of victory. He was glad Ebenezer was his friend. The blacksmith finished with the mare's last foot, dropping it gently to the floor. "There you are, Daisy. Good as new."

Her owner paid the blacksmith and led her out. She did not so much as glance at Twinkleheels as she left, but she held her head so high that she nearly bumped it on the door frame.

"Well, Ebenezer," the smith said, wiping his hands on his leather apron. "Let's see about that shoe you cast. Is it just the one?"

"Just the one," Farmer Green answered for him. "But the others are well worn. You may as well give him a full set while he's here."

"Sounds wise," the smith agreed. He untied Ebenezer from the ring and led him to the center of the floor. "You know what to do, old friend."

Ebenezer stood as quiet as a statue while the smith went to work. Twinkleheels watched everything, his earlier fears now mixed with a great deal of curiosity. The smith took a heavy tool with a hooked end and pried off Ebenezer's three old shoes, one by one. Then, with a special knife, he trimmed the edges of Ebenezer's hoofs, just as a person might trim his fingernails. He made it look very easy, and Ebenezer did not even flinch.

Then came the part that had worried Twinkleheels. The smith went to the fiery forge and pulled out a glowing, red hot horseshoe with a long pair of tongs. He carried it to the anvil and with a great *clang, clang, CLANG* he hammered it, sending a shower of bright sparks into the air. Twinkleheels wanted to jump, but he saw how calm Ebenezer was, and he made himself stand still.

The smith brought the hot shoe over to Ebenezer. For just a moment, he pressed it against the trimmed hoof. A puff of white smoke rose up with a sharp, strange smell and a quick *Tsssssssss* sound. Twinkleheels' eyes grew wide. He was sure that must have hurt terribly! But Ebenezer only shifted his weight a little, as if a fly had landed on him. He seemed not to mind at all.

"Just checking the fit," the smith said, more to Johnnie than to the horses. He took the shoe to the tub of water and dropped it in. A great cloud of steam hissed up to the rafters. After it was cool, he took Ebenezer's foot again and began to nail the new shoe in place. *Tap. Tap. Tap.* The little nails went in so easily. The smith was very careful, and when he was done, he filed the ends of the nails so they were smooth.

He did the same for all four of Ebenezer's feet. The whole time, the old horse stood patiently, occasionally swishing his tail. When the smith was finished, he patted Ebenezer on the neck. "There you go, old timer. Ready for another hundred miles."

Ebenezer took a step, and his newly shod hoof made a crisp, solid sound on the dirt floor.

"Now then," the smith said, turning his kind eyes toward Twinkleheels. "It's the little fellow's turn."

Johnnie Green came and untied Twinkleheels' halter rope. "Come on, Twinkleheels," he said softly, giving him a gentle tug. "It's your turn to be a big horse."

Twinkleheels' heart began to beat a little faster. It was one thing to watch wise old Ebenezer. It was quite another to be the one standing in the middle of the floor with the big smith. He took a few steps forward and then stopped. He looked at the forge, and the anvil, and the tub of water. It all seemed very alarming again.

"He's a bit timid," Farmer Green said. "This is his first time."

"They often are," the smith said with a smile. "Don't you worry, pony. We'll take good care of you." He walked slowly towards Twinkleheels and held out the back of his hand for him to sniff. It smelled of iron and smoke and horses. Twinkleheels stretched his neck and gave it a cautious sniff.

"There now," the smith said. "We're friends already. Now, let's have a look at this left front foot."

Twinkleheels wasn't sure what to do. He remembered his conversation with Ebenezer and felt a bit foolish. Which foot was he supposed to lift? He shuffled nervously.

The smith seemed to understand. He ran his hand down Twinkleheels' leg and then gently but firmly cupped his hand around the pony's ankle. "Up we go," he said, and lifted the foot. Twinkleheels instinctively pulled back, but Johnnie was right there, stroking his neck. "Easy, boy. Easy. He won't hurt you."

Twinkleheels decided to be brave. He let the smith hold his foot. The man cradled the hoof in his lap and examined it. "Never had a shoe on him, that's clear," he murmured. "Good, healthy foot, though. Won't need much trimming."

He set the foot down and went to a rack on the wall. He came back with a very small, new horseshoe. He held it against Twinkleheels' hoof to measure it. "A little wide," he said. "We'll have to shape it."

Twinkleheels watched him carry the little shoe to the forge. He watched him heat it until it glowed like a cherry. He watched him pound it on the anvil, making a much lighter, quicker *ting, ting, TING* sound than he had for Ebenezer's big shoes. His fear was turning into fascination.

When the smith came back with the hot shoe, Twinkleheels trembled. Johnnie's hand was a comforting weight on his withers. "Stand now," Johnnie whispered. "Like Ebenezer did."

Twinkleheels squeezed his eyes shut. He felt the smith lift his foot. He smelled that sharp, smoky smell getting closer. Then he heard the *Tssssss* and felt a strange warmth through his hoof, but no pain at all! It was the most surprising thing. He opened his eyes just as the smith took the shoe away.

"Perfect fit," the smith declared, and went to cool the shoe in the water tub.

A moment later he was back, ready to nail it on. Twinkleheels felt the first tap of the hammer. *Tap.* He flinched. "Whoa, son," the smith said calmly. *Tap, tap.* Twinkleheels held his breath. It didn't hurt. It was just a funny, jarring feeling. *Tap, tap, tap.* The smith drove in six tiny nails, and then it was over. He filed the ends smooth.

"There," he said, and gently placed Twinkleheels' foot back on the ground. "One down, three to go."

The foot felt strange. It felt heavy. When the smith moved on to his other front foot, Twinkleheels found it was much easier. He knew what to expect now. He held up his foot willingly. He barely noticed the smoke this time, and the sound of the nailing was almost comforting.

By the time the smith started on his hind feet, Twinkleheels was feeling quite proud of himself. He stood as still as Ebenezer had. He felt like a veteran. He was a pony who knew all about blacksmith shops. When the last nail was driven into his fourth and final shoe, he felt a great sense of accomplishment.

"All done!" the smith announced, giving Twinkleheels a friendly slap on the rump. "You were a fine customer. Stood better than Daisy did, and she's been coming here for years."

Johnnie Green led him away from the center of the floor. "Go on, try them out," he said.

Twinkleheels took a careful step. *Clink.* The sound was new and wonderful. He took another step. *Clank.* It was loud and important on the hard floor. He lifted his front feet high, one after the other, just to hear the noise they made when they came down. He walked in a small circle, his head up, his ears forward. He felt taller. He felt stronger.

"Look at him strut!" Farmer Green said with a laugh. "He's as proud as a peacock with his new shoes."

Twinkleheels was proud. He walked right over to Ebenezer, who was now hitched to the buggy again. *Clink, clank, clink, clank.* It was the best sound he had ever heard.

"Well?" Ebenezer said, looking down at him. "How does it feel to be a gentleman of the road?"

"It feels wonderful!" Twinkleheels exclaimed. "They are a bit heavy, but I like the sound they make! I feel very grand!"

Farmer Green paid the smith, and then he and Johnnie climbed into the buggy. Johnnie still held Twinkleheels' halter. "Come on, Twinkleheels. Time to go home."

Twinkleheels followed them out of the dim smithy and into the bright, snowy world. The sound his new shoes made on the village street was even better. It was a crisp, sharp *clip-clop-clip-clop* that echoed off the buildings. He had heard horses make that sound all his life, and now he was making it too!

He trotted happily behind the buggy, his head high. He did not mind matching Ebenezer's steady pace at all. He was too busy listening to his own feet.

"You see," Ebenezer said as they left the village behind and started down the road to the farm. "There was nothing to fear."

"I know that now," Twinkleheels admitted. "But I am glad you were with me. That white mare was not very kind."

"Some horses are like that," the old horse said wisely. "They think puffing themselves up makes them look bigger, but it only shows how empty they are inside. You were brave, and that is what matters. You stood your ground and you earned your shoes."

Twinkleheels felt a warm glow of pride. "Do the shoes help you go faster?" he asked.

Ebenezer chuckled. "No, not faster. But they help you grip the icy roads. And they keep your hoofs from wearing down on the hard stones. They let you do your work without getting sore. They are a tool, just like a harness or a plow. A good tool for a good horse."

Twinkleheels thought about that. He was not just a pony for playing in the pasture anymore. He was a pony with tools. He was a working pony.

When they turned into the lane that led to the farmhouse, old dog Spot came bounding out to meet them, barking a welcome. He stopped short, his head cocked to one side.

"What is that new noise?" he barked. "That clicky-clacky sound! Is there a stranger with you?"

"No, Spot!" Johnnie Green called out. "It's just Twinkleheels! He has new shoes!"

Twinkleheels stopped and proudly lifted a foot for Spot to see. Spot came close and sniffed at the iron shoe curiously. He let out a little yip of surprise and then began to run in excited circles around the pony.

Farmer Green drove the buggy right to the barn door. Johnnie jumped out and unhitched Ebenezer, then led both horses inside. The warm barn was filled with the sweet smell of hay. The two bay horses, who had been brought in from the pasture, looked over their stall doors as they entered.

"Well, look who's back," said one of them. "Did you enjoy your fancy trip to town, little one?"

"I had a very fine time," Twinkleheels replied. His voice sounded different to his own ears. It sounded more mature. He walked past their stalls, and the sound of his new shoes on the wooden plank floor was loud and confident. *Clack! Clack! Clack! Clack!*

The two bays watched him go by, their eyes wide. They did not seem to have a teasing remark ready. They just stared as Johnnie led the proud little pony to his own stall.

Johnnie filled his manger with fresh, sweet-smelling hay and made sure his water bucket was full. He gave Twinkleheels one last pat. "You were a good boy today, Twinkleheels. A very brave boy."

Twinkleheels watched him leave, then turned to his hay. He was tired from the excitement of the day, but he felt wonderful. He looked across at Ebenezer, who was quietly munching in the next stall.

"Thank you, Ebenezer," Twinkleheels said softly. "I would have been very frightened today if you had not been there to explain things."

The old horse nodded his head slowly. "You are welcome, Twinkleheels," he said. "But you were the one who had to stand still for the smith. You did that all by yourself. You are growing up."

Twinkleheels took a long drink of cool water. He could feel the solid, steady weight of the iron on his feet. It felt right. He was not just Twinkleheels the pasture pony anymore. He was Twinkleheels, the shod pony, ready for any road at all. And he thought that was a very fine thing to be.

Twinkleheels held his breath. He felt the little taps, but there was no pain. Not even a prickle. The smith drove in several nails, and then with a quick twist of his tool, he bent the ends over and filed them smooth. He did the same with the other three feet. Twinkleheels was so surprised that it was all over so quickly and easily that he forgot to be timid.

"There now!" the blacksmith declared, giving Twinkleheels a friendly slap on the shoulder. "A fine set of shoes for a fine little pony. You're ready for the road now!"

Farmer Green paid the man, and Johnnie led Twinkleheels toward the wide doorway. When his new iron shoes touched the hard-packed dirt floor, they made a sound he had never made before. A solid, clicking, clacking sound. It was a wonderful sound! It was the sound of a grown-up, working horse!

Ebenezer followed him out into the bright winter sunshine. "Well," the old horse said. "How does it feel to be shod?"

"It feels splendid!" Twinkleheels exclaimed. "I feel taller! And my feet feel so strong and steady!" He took a few steps, just to hear the noise again. *Click-clack. Click-clack.* "Why did I ever worry?"

Ebenezer smiled his slow, wise smile. "Most worries are bigger in our minds than they are in the world," he said. "Shoes are a good thing, Twinkleheels, especially on these icy roads. And they keep your hoofs from wearing down on the hard stones. They let you do your work without getting sore. They are a tool, just like a harness or a plow. A good tool for a good horse."

Twinkleheels thought about that. He was not just a pony for playing in the pasture anymore. He was a pony with tools. He was a working pony.

When they turned into the lane that led to the farmhouse, old dog Spot came bounding out to meet them, barking a welcome. He stopped short, his head cocked to one side.

"What is that new noise?" he barked. "That clicky-clacky sound! Is there a stranger with you?"

"No, Spot!" Johnnie Green called out. "It's just Twinkleheels! He has new shoes!"

Twinkleheels stopped and proudly lifted a foot for Spot to see. Spot came close and sniffed at the iron shoe curiously. He let out a little yip of surprise and then began to run in excited circles around the pony.

Farmer Green drove the buggy right to the barn door. Johnnie jumped out and unhitched Ebenezer, then led both horses inside. The warm barn was filled with the sweet smell of hay. The two bay horses, who had been brought in from the pasture, looked over their stall doors as they entered.

"Well, look who's back," said one of them. "Did you enjoy your fancy trip to town, little one?"

"I had a very fine time," Twinkleheels replied. His voice sounded different to his own ears. It sounded more mature. He walked past their stalls, and the sound of his new shoes on the wooden plank floor was loud and confident. *Clack! Clack! Clack! Clack!*

The two bays watched him go by, their eyes wide. They did not seem to have a teasing remark ready. They just stared as Johnnie led the proud little pony to his own stall.

Johnnie filled his manger with fresh, sweet-smelling hay and made sure his water bucket was full. He gave Twinkleheels one last pat. "You were a good boy today, Twinkleheels. A very brave boy."

Twinkleheels watched him leave, then turned to his hay. He was tired from the excitement of the day, but he felt wonderful. He looked across at Ebenezer, who was quietly munching in the next stall.

"Thank you, Ebenezer," Twinkleheels said softly. "I would have been very frightened today if you had not been there to explain things."

The old horse nodded his head slowly. "You are welcome, Twinkleheels," he said. "But you were the one who had to stand still for the smith. You did that all by yourself. You are growing up."

Twinkleheels took a long drink of cool water. He could feel the solid, steady weight of the iron on his feet. It felt right. He was not just Twinkleheels the pasture pony anymore. He was Twinkleheels, the shod pony, ready for any road at all. And he thought that was a very fine thing to be.

XVII A NEW SOUND

For the rest of the afternoon, Twinkleheels found excuses to move about in his stall. He would walk to his water bucket for a drink he did not need. He would shift from one side of his stall to the other, just for the pleasure of hearing the crisp *clack!* of iron on wood. It was a most satisfying sound.

The two bay horses in the stalls down the way had recovered from their surprise.

"Listen to him," one of them, whose name was Flash, snickered to his brother, Dash. "He sounds like a woodpecker drumming on a frozen log."

"He sounds like a tin can full of pebbles," Dash replied with a whinny of laughter. "All that noise for such a little pony!"

Twinkleheels heard them, but for once he did not feel a sting of annoyance. He felt only pity for them. They had worn shoes for so long that they had forgotten the thrill of it. They did not appreciate the fine, important sound they made.

"It is the sound of a horse who has been to the village," Twinkleheels called back to them, his voice full of dignity. "It is the sound of a horse who can travel on hard roads."

"Oh, listen to him!" Flash neighed. "He gets four little bits of iron nailed to his feet and suddenly he thinks he is a stagecoach leader!"

Old Ebenezer, who had been dozing, opened one eye. "Let him be proud, Flash," he rumbled. "It is a big day for him. Do you not remember your first shoes?"

Flash flicked his ears back. "It was a long time ago," he said, though not as boastfully as before. "I suppose I was proud, too." But then he looked at Twinkleheels again and could not resist one more jab. "But I did not make such a racket about it!"

Twinkleheels ignored him. He was listening to Ebenezer. "You must be careful with those shoes, Twinkleheels," the old horse said quietly. "They can help you on the ice, it is true. They give you a better grip than a bare hoof. But they can also slip if you are not cautious. Ice is a treacherous thing. It does not care how proud you are."

"I will be careful," Twinkleheels promised. But in his heart, he felt that Ebenezer was being a little too cautious. With these wonderful iron shoes, what was there to fear from a little ice? He felt he could trot up a frozen waterfall if he chose.

The next morning, the air was sharp and cold, and the sun shone so brightly on the snow that it made you squint. Johnnie Green came into the barn with a cheerful "Good morning!" for everyone. He carried a small basket in his hand.

"Father says I can go to the village store for Mother," he told the horses as he measured out their morning oats. "She needs some thread for her sewing. And since the main road is cleared, he said I could take a horse."

Twinkleheels' heart gave a little leap. A trip to the village! On the hard road!

Johnnie came to his stall first. "I think I'll take you, Twinkleheels," he said, stroking the pony's neck. "It's not a heavy load, just me and this little basket. And you need to get used to your new shoes on a real road."

Twinkleheels could have burst with joy! He nudged Johnnie's shoulder and whinnied eagerly.

As Johnnie was putting on his bridle, Farmer Green came into the barn. "Now, Johnnie," he said, "I have another errand. I need these bags of feed taken over to Mr. Henderson's farm. It is on the same road, just past the village crossroads. I will hitch up Flash and Dash to the light sleigh. You two can travel together."

A sleigh! With Flash and Dash! Twinkleheels' ears perked up. This was getting more interesting by the minute.

Flash and Dash looked very pleased with themselves as Farmer Green backed them into the shafts of the sleigh. It was a handsome sleigh, painted red, with little bells on the harness that jingled merrily.

"We will get there in no time," Dash boasted to his brother. "A sleigh slides so easily over the snowpack."

"We will be there and back before the little pony has even passed the big oak tree," Flash added, tossing his mane.

As they were all led out into the bright, cold barnyard, Farmer Green gave his final instructions. "Now, listen to me, both of you," he said, looking from the sleigh to Johnnie on Twinkleheels' back. "You stay together. And Johnnie, you keep that pony at a steady trot. The center of the road is mostly gravel and packed snow, but there are patches of sheer ice near the edges from the melting and freezing. No foolishness. No racing."

"Yes, Father," Johnnie said.

But Twinkleheels barely heard the warning. All he could hear was the boast of the bays and the exciting jingle of the sleigh bells. A race! Farmer Green had said not to, but what could be the harm in a little friendly contest? With his new shoes, he was sure he could beat the big sleigh easily.

XVIII A FOOLISH CHALLENGE

They set off down the long farm lane, Twinkleheels and Johnnie in the lead, and the sleigh with Flash and Dash jingling along behind them. The sound of Twinkleheels' new shoes on the packed snow of the lane was a crisp, satisfying *crunch-click, crunch-click*.

When they reached the main road, the feeling was different. Here, the snow had been packed down hard by sleighs and wagons, and in some places, the wind had swept it clean, revealing the frozen, stony ground beneath. And just as Farmer Green had warned, there were glistening patches along the sides of the road that looked like dark, wet glass. That was the black ice.

"Easy now, Twinkleheels," Johnnie said, holding a firm rein. He kept the pony right in the middle of the road, where the footing was best.

For the first mile, they went along at a sensible trot. But Twinkleheels could feel the sleigh close behind him. He could hear the bays snorting, and the sound seemed to be full of impatience and mockery.

"Is this as fast as he can go?" he heard Dash mutter. "My grandmother could walk faster than this!"

"Hush!" said the farmhand who was driving them. "Farmer Green said to take it easy."

But the words were spoken. Twinkleheels' pride, which was already puffed up like a robin's chest, felt a sharp prick. He gave a little pull on the reins, wanting to go faster.

"Whoa, boy," Johnnie murmured, holding him back.

Just then, the sleigh pulled alongside them. Flash turned his head and looked down his long nose at Twinkleheels. "Having trouble keeping up, little one?" he neighed. "Perhaps you need another set of shoes to help you."

That was too much for Twinkleheels to bear. He forgot all about Farmer Green's warning. He forgot Ebenezer's wise words about caution. All he could think about was showing those boastful bays what a pony with new shoes could do. He tossed his head and gave a challenging snort, right back at Flash.

Johnnie, too, was feeling the spirit of competition. He was a boy, after all, and the sight of the handsome sleigh beside them made him want to race. "Do you think we can beat them to the crossroads, Twinkleheels?" he whispered.

Twinkleheels answered by stretching out his neck and quickening his pace without any urging. He broke from a trot into a canter, and the *click-clack* of his hoofs became a rapid, drumming beat on the hard road.

"Johnnie! You stop that!" the farmhand called from the sleigh.

But Johnnie only laughed. "Catch us if you can!" he shouted back over his shoulder.

The race was on!

Twinkleheels had never felt so wonderful. The cold air rushed past his ears. The road flew by beneath his feet. And the new shoes! They felt magical. They bit into the packed snow and gravel, giving him a purchase he had never known before. He felt as if he were flying.

He pulled ahead of the sleigh. The jingling of its bells grew fainter behind him. He glanced back. The two big bay horses were pulling hard, their heads low, but the sleigh was heavy and they could not match his burst of speed.

"We're winning, Twinkleheels! We're winning!" Johnnie cried, his face flushed with excitement.

Twinkleheels' heart swelled with triumph. He would show them all! He would show Flash and Dash, and even old Ebenezer, that these shoes made him the fastest horse on the farm. He was not just a small pony. He was a champion!

The crossroads were just ahead, marked by a big, leafless maple tree. Victory was only a few hundred yards away. The sleigh was falling farther and farther behind. Twinkleheels felt he had energy to spare. He thought he would show off just a little more.

Instead of staying in the safe middle of the road, he decided to cut the corner, to make his victory even more impressive. The turn was wide, and the inside curve was a smooth, dark, glistening sheet of ice.

He never even saw it coming.

XIX SLIPPERY PRIDE

One moment, Twinkleheels was the king of the road, his feet drumming a triumphant rhythm. The next moment, the world dissolved into a bewildering, terrifying slide.

His front feet, which had been gripping the road so bravely, suddenly found nothing to hold on to. The hard, wonderful iron shoes that had given him so much confidence became his enemies. They were as slick as butter on a hot pan.

His legs flew out from under him. For one heart-stopping second, he seemed to hang in the air, a jumble of legs and flying snow. Johnnie gave a cry of alarm and tumbled from his back, landing softly and safely in a deep snowdrift at the side of the road.

*CRASH!*

Twinkleheels came down hard. His side struck the icy road with a painful jolt that knocked the wind right out of him. He lay there, stunned and dazed, listening to the sleigh with Flash and Dash clatter past. They did not make a sound, no mocking whinny, no boastful cry. There was only the sound of their hoofs and the frantic jingle of the bells as the farmhand pulled them to a stop a short way down the road.

Twinkleheels scrambled, trying to get up. But his situation was worse now than it had been in the snowdrift. There, the snow had been soft but yielding. Here, the ice was hard but offered no grip at all. Every time he tried to get a foot under him, the iron shoe would just skate away. He flailed and struggled, his metal-shod hoofs making a dreadful, scraping noise on the ice. It was a useless, frightening dance.

"Twinkleheels!" Johnnie cried, scrambling out of the snowbank. He ran to the pony's side, his face white with fear. "Are you hurt, boy? Are you hurt?"

Twinkleheels was not badly hurt. He was bruised and sore, and his pride was shattered into a thousand pieces. But more than that, he was scared. He could not get up. He was trapped and helpless on the very road he had thought he had conquered. He let out a low, miserable whinny.

The farmhand had jumped down from the sleigh and was running back towards them. "Are you all right, Johnnie?" he called.

"I'm fine!" Johnnie answered, his voice trembling a little. "But Twinkleheels has fallen! He can't get up!"

The farmhand reached them and looked down at the pony struggling on the ice. He shook his head. "This is what your father was afraid of," he said grimly. "Racing on an icy road. It's a fool's game."

Twinkleheels stopped struggling and lay still. The word "fool" echoed in his ears. That was what he was. A proud, silly fool. He had ignored every warning. He had thought his new shoes made him invincible, but they had only made his fall harder and his predicament worse. He laid his head down on the cold, hard ice and wished he could disappear. He was so ashamed he could not even look at Johnnie.

The two bay horses, Flash and Dash, watched from a distance. They were very quiet. There was no triumph in their posture. They just stood with their heads drooping, looking at the small pony lying on the ice. Perhaps they were remembering that it could just as easily have been one of them.

"We have to get him up," the farmhand said. "But he'll never find his footing on this sheet. Wait here."

He ran to the side of the road and began scooping up handfuls of gravel and dirt from beneath the snow. He came back and scattered it all around Twinkleheels' feet, creating a gritty, rough surface on top of the treacherous ice.

"Now, boy," he said to Twinkleheels in a firm but not unkind voice. "Try again. Slowly."

With Johnnie pulling gently on his bridle and the farmhand giving him a push from behind, Twinkleheels made another attempt. This time, his iron shoes found a grip on the scattered gravel. With a great heave and a groan, he managed to get his legs underneath him. He wobbled for a moment, like a newborn foal, and then he was standing.

He stood there, trembling all over, not from cold, but from fright and shame. His coat was scuffed and dirty on one side. One of his knees had a small scrape. But the deepest wound was to his pride.

Johnnie threw his arms around the pony's neck. "Oh, Twinkleheels," he said. "I'm so sorry. It was my fault, too. I shouldn't have let you run."

Twinkleheels just leaned against the boy, grateful for his kindness. The grand race was over. And he had lost more than just a contest of speed.

XX A LESSON LEARNED

The journey home was very different from the journey out. There was no more talk of racing. The farmhand led the sleigh, and Johnnie walked beside Twinkleheels, leading him by the reins. The pony limped a little, and the proud *clack-clack* of his shoes was gone. In its place was a slow, hesitant *clink... clank...* that sounded sad and sorry.

Flash and Dash followed quietly behind, without a single boastful snort between them. They seemed to understand that a lesson had been learned by everyone that morning.

When they turned into the farm lane, Farmer Green was waiting for them. He had a stern look on his face. He had clearly been watching from the house.

"Johnnie Green," he said, his voice low and serious. "What did I tell you before you left?"

Johnnie looked down at his boots. "You told us not to race, Father," he mumbled. "I'm sorry. We got carried away. Twinkleheels fell."

Farmer Green came over and ran his hands expertly over Twinkleheels' legs and side. He examined the scrape on his knee. "It's not a bad fall," he declared, "but it could have been. A pony could break a leg this way. And you, Johnnie, could have been seriously hurt. Pride is a poor reason to risk your neck, or your pony's."

He looked from his son to the little pony. Twinkleheels drooped his head, expecting a scolding.

"And you, young man," Farmer Green said to Twinkleheels, his voice a bit softer. "I expect you've learned something about ice and iron shoes today."

Twinkleheels could only nod his head miserably.

Farmer Green sighed. "Well, a lesson learned the hard way is often a lesson that sticks. Let's get you into the barn and get that scrape cleaned up."

Inside the warm, hay-scented barn, Twinkleheels felt a great sense of relief. He was safe. Farmer Green cleaned his scraped knee with a gentle hand and put some salve on it. Johnnie gave him an extra helping of sweet oats, stroking his neck the whole time.

When they were alone, Twinkleheels looked across at Ebenezer's stall. The old horse was watching him with his kind, deep-set eyes. He did not say, "I told you so." He did not need to.

"I was foolish, Ebenezer," Twinkleheels said in a small voice. "I thought my new shoes made me better than everyone. I thought I could not fall."

"Ah," said Ebenezer, nodding slowly. "That is a mistake many young ones make. They get a little bit of strength, or a little bit of speed, and they think they have no more need for caution. But a truly strong horse, Twinkleheels, is a horse that respects the road he travels on. He knows where to step, and when to slow down."

He took a mouthful of hay and chewed it thoughtfully. "Those shoes are good tools," he continued. "But a hammer is no good without a smart carpenter to swing it. And shoes are no good without a smart horse to wear them. They do not think for you. They only help you do what you have already decided to do. If you decide to be foolish, they will help you be foolish all the faster."

"Oh?" Ebenezer said, his ears twitching with interest. "And what was the best part?"

Ebenezer nodded his great head slowly. "That it does," he agreed. "That it does. A ribbon fades. Trust, if you tend to it, only grows stronger. It is the finest harness a horse and his master can share."

Twinkleheels and Ebenezer both poked their heads farther out of the barn to see. The trailer was not like the simple, sturdy ones they sometimes saw going to market. This one was long and sleek, painted a gleaming silver, with fancy lettering on the side that they couldn't quite read from this distance.

"Well, I'll be," Farmer Green said, wiping his hands on a rag as he came from the workshop. "Looks like we have new neighbors. Let's go and say how-do, Johnnie."

"That's Gallant Prince," Johnnie whispered to Twinkleheels, stroking his neck. "His owner is a Mr. Sterling, from the city. He says Prince is a champion show horse."

The sun finally set, and the woods became a place of deep shadows and strange shapes. A cool wind began to whisper through the treetops, making a sound like a long, sad sigh. Johnnie slid off Twinkleheels' back.

"We will have to stay here for the night," the boy said, his voice barely a whisper. "Father will come looking for us in the morning." He wrapped his arms around the pony's neck, and Twinkleheels could feel him shivering. It might have been from the cold, or it might have been from fear.

Twinkleheels stood perfectly still, letting Johnnie hold on to him. He felt the boy's warmth, and it was the only comfort in the cold, dark woods. He was no hero. He was just a lost and foolish little pony who had made a terrible mistake. He pressed his head against Johnnie's shoulder, as if to say, "I am sorry."

He thought of his warm, safe stall in the barn. He thought of the sweet smell of hay and the comforting presence of old Ebenezer in the next stall. He had been so eager to leave it all behind for an adventure. Now, he would have given anything to be back there.

An owl hooted somewhere in the darkness, a long, mournful sound that seemed to ask, "Who? Who are you?"

Twinkleheels did not have an answer. He did not feel like Twinkleheels the Hero anymore. He did not know who he was at all. He just knew that he was scared, and that it was the longest, darkest night of his life.

XX A HUMBLING JOURNEY

Back at the farm, the sun had set and there was no sign of Johnnie and Twinkleheels. Farmer Green stood on the porch, his face a grim mask of worry as he scanned the dark line of the North Woods.

"They should have been back hours ago," he said to his wife, who stood twisting her apron in her hands. "The boy knows better than to be out after dark."

Farmer Green wasted no more time. He strode to the barn, his lantern swinging and casting long, dancing shadows. "Ebenezer!" he called, his voice sharp with urgency. "We have work to do."

The old horse, who had been dozing, was instantly awake. He knew that tone in his master's voice. It meant trouble.

As Farmer Green quickly put on the harness, he called to the farmhand. "Tom! Saddle up Flash and Dash! They are fast. We will need to cover a lot of ground."

The two bay horses, hearing this, pricked up their ears. They had heard the commotion and knew that Johnnie and the pony were missing. For a moment, a flicker of mean satisfaction went through them. The little show-off had finally gotten himself into a mess.

But then they saw the look on Farmer Green's face. And they saw old Ebenezer, his expression grave, being hitched to the buggy. This was not a game. This was serious.

"Listen to me, you two," Farmer Green said, looking them straight in the eye. "I know you can run. I have seen you do it when you were not supposed to. Tonight, I want you to run for a reason. We will search the trails. You will call out. Johnnie will know your whinnies. Do you understand?"

Flash and Dash looked at each other. They were being asked to help find the very pony they had been sneering at all week. But they were also being trusted with an important job. They nodded their heads, their flightiness replaced by a new sense of purpose.

The search party set out. Farmer Green and Ebenezer took the main logging trail, the lantern light cutting a small, brave circle in the vast darkness. Tom, on Flash, and another farmhand on Dash, took the side paths, their powerful legs eating up the ground.

"Johnnie!" Farmer Green called out, his voice echoing among the trees. "Twinkleheels!"

Flash and Dash did their part, letting out loud, clear whinnies that carried far in the still night air.

Meanwhile, deep in the woods, Johnnie and Twinkleheels heard the faint sounds. At first, Johnnie thought he was dreaming. "Did you hear that?" he whispered, lifting his head from Twinkleheels' neck.

Twinkleheels' ears swiveled, straining to catch the sound again. There it was! A horse's call! And it sounded familiar. It sounded like... Flash!

He wanted to answer, but his throat was tight with shame. What if they laughed at him? What if they said, "We told you so"?

But then he heard another sound, a man's voice, faint but clear. "Johnnie!"

"It is Father!" Johnnie cried, scrambling to his feet. "They are looking for us! Father! We are over here! Father!"

His voice was small against the vastness of the woods. Twinkleheels knew it would not carry far. He had to help. Forgetting his pride, forgetting his shame, he lifted his head and let out the loudest, most desperate whinny of his life. It was not the proud nicker of a hero. It was the frightened cry of a lost pony who needed help.

A moment later, an answering call came back, much closer this time. Then they saw it: a light, bobbing through the trees. Soon, Flash, with Tom on his back, burst into their small, miserable clearing. The big bay horse had never been a more welcome sight.

The journey home was quiet. Johnnie rode on Flash, bundled in a blanket Tom had brought, while the farmhand led a very subdued Twinkleheels by the halter. They met Farmer Green and Ebenezer on the trail. Farmer Green did not scold. He just lifted Johnnie down, held him tight for a long moment, and then put him in the buggy beside him.

Back in the warm, bright barn, Twinkleheels was led to his stall. He hung his head, not daring to look at anyone. He felt the eyes of the other horses on him. He had never felt so small.

A few minutes later, Ebenezer's familiar, kind face appeared over the top of the stall door. He did not say "I told you so." He did not say anything for a long moment. He just looked at Twinkleheels with his wise, steady eyes.

"The North Woods is a tricky place," the old horse said at last, his voice soft. "It has humbled bigger horses than you, little one."

A tear trickled down Twinkleheels' nose and fell onto the straw. "I was foolish, Ebenezer," he whispered. "I was so full of pride. I thought I knew better than anyone."

"Pride is a poor map to follow," Ebenezer agreed gently. "It will always lead you to a place where you are all alone. Sometimes," he added, "the bravest thing a horse can do is admit he is lost, and ask for help."

Twinkleheels looked up. Through the barn door, he could see Flash and Dash being rubbed down. They had run hard, and their coats were dark with sweat. They had helped save him.

The next morning, Johnnie came to the stall. He did not bring any of his friends. He just carried a brush and a soft cloth. He did not say a word as he began to groom Twinkleheels, his hands gentle and sure.

"I was proud too," Johnnie said quietly, after a while. "I thought because you were brave once, you would be brave always, and never make a mistake. But that is not fair. We are a team. We are supposed to help each other."

He put his arms around the pony's neck. "I am just glad you are safe."

Twinkleheels leaned into the boy's embrace. The praise of the neighborhood children had felt good for a time, but it was a fleeting, hollow thing. This feeling, this quiet bond of forgiveness and friendship, was real. It was a prize far greater than any ribbon, and a lesson he knew he would carry inside him forever.
